title: Digital literacy is not what we think it is.
subtitle: The next digital skill isn’t technical. It’s judgement.
idea: Digital literacy isn’t knowing which buttons to press. It’s judging whether to trust what AI gives you.
try: Ask your manager what AI training your Trust offers, and raise it at your next supervision or team meeting.
watch: AI sounds just as confident when it’s wrong. Patient identifiable information never goes into a consumer AI tool.

title: The tool the NHS is committing to.
subtitle: You do not have to prefer Copilot. You do need to understand it.
idea: The NHS is committing to Copilot. You don’t have to prefer it, but you do need to understand it.
try: Sign in with your Trust account and try one small task, like summarising a meeting note you wrote.
watch: An approved tool doesn’t move responsibility. You’re still accountable for what you put in, so check your Trust’s guidance first.

title: The first Copilot app worth a proper look.
subtitle: I took a 20 page workflow into OneNote to see what its Copilot features could actually do.
idea: OneNote’s Copilot Notebooks sits inside your Trust’s system, so it suits Trust material that can’t go into consumer AI.
try: Upload one low-risk document, like a guideline or an email trail, and see what it does with it.
watch: How it stores your uploads isn’t clear yet. Don’t upload anything you wouldn’t want a colleague outside your team to read.

title: The AI tool that lives on your phone.
subtitle: No cloud. No account. Works offline. Nothing leaves your device.
idea: Open source AI that runs on your phone. Because it’s local, it works offline and your questions stay on the device.
try: Download PocketPal, pick a pal and ask it one question you’d normally ask ChatGPT. Compare the answers.
watch: Local doesn’t mean cleared. Patient identifiable information still goes into no AI tool, and smaller models make more mistakes.

title: Made with, alongside, or by AI?
subtitle: Where does your work end and the machine’s begin?
idea: “Was AI used?” is too blunt. Ask where the important decisions came from: made with, alongside or by AI.
try: Next time you use AI, say how: “I wrote it and used AI to edit the language.”
watch: Automation bias. An AI draft is easier to approve than to check. Sometimes the friction is the thinking.

title: The email was sent. But who’s doing the job?
subtitle: A tool can track the task. Someone still has to do it.
idea: Agreed actions slip because nobody is tracking them. Sending the email isn’t the same as doing the job.
try: Open Planner on your Trust account. Take three actions from your last meeting and give each an owner and a date.
watch: Task names can carry identifiable information. Use composite wording and link to documents rather than pasting them in.
